(p-182) Surah al-Hijr: ninety-nine verses, Meccan.

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

﴿Alif, Lam, Ra. These are the verses of the Book, and of a clear Qur'an.﴾ "Tilka" (those) is a pointer to the verses that this surah contains. "Al-Kitab" (the Book) and "al-Qur'an al-Mubin" (the clear Qur'an) refer to the surah. The indefinite form of "Qur'an" is for magnification. The meaning is: these are the verses of the Book that is perfect in being a Book, and [the verses of] a clear Qur'an. As if it were said: the Book that gathers perfection and wondrous eloquence in its clarity.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 15, verse 2:

﴿Rubama﴾ with the light pronunciation (takhfif): Madani and ʿAsim; with the heavy pronunciation (tashdid): the others. The "ma" here is the kaffa (the "ma" that "restrains" the particle), because rubba is a particle that governs the noun following it and is specific to an indefinite noun (nakira). When it is restrained by ma, the past verb and the noun may follow it. The phrase ﴿Those who disbelieve will wish﴾ is permissible because what is expected (al-mutarraqqab) in God Most High's reports is in the position of the past tense, certain in its realization. It is as if it were said: "Perhaps he wished." Their wishing will occur at the time of the dispute (al-nizaʿ), or on the Day of Resurrection, when they see their own state and the state of the Muslims; or when they see the Muslims coming out of the Fire, so the disbeliever wishes that he had been a Muslim. This is related from Ibn ʿAbbas, may God be pleased with them both. ﴿Had they been Muslims﴾ is the report of their wishing. It has been brought in the third-person form (lafz al-ghayba) because they are being reported about, as when you say: "He swore by God that he would certainly do it," and it would not be right to say "He swore that I would certainly do it." And "If only we had been Muslims" would have been good. It is reduced by "rubba" because the terrors of the Resurrection occupy them from wishing; then when they recover from the agonies of punishment, they wish that they had been Muslims. As for the view of one who says that "rubba" is meant to express abundance, it is an error, because it is the opposite of what the people of the language know, since it was established for diminishment (al-taqlil).

﴿Leave them﴾, an imperative of contempt (ʾamr ihānah), meaning: cut off your hope of their turning back, leave them alone from forbidding them what they are upon, and from turning them away from it through reminder and advice. ﴿Let them eat and enjoy themselves﴾ with their worldly life, ﴿and let hope distract them﴾, that is, let their hopes and wishes occupy them away from faith. ﴿But they will soon know﴾ the evil of their conduct. In this is an alert that preferring pleasure and luxury, and what leads to them such as long hope, is not among the characteristics of the believers.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 15, verse 4:

﴿And We did not destroy any town but that it had a decreed term known (to Us).﴾ "And it had a decreed term" (wa-lahā kitābun) is a clause (jumlah) in the position of a qualifier (ṣifah) for "town" (qaryah). By analogy (qiyās), the waw should not intervene between them, as in ﴿And We did not destroy any town but that it had warners.﴾ [al-Shu'arā': 208] The waw has intervened only to emphasize the attachment of the qualifier to the qualified, since the qualifier is attached to the qualified without a waw. So the waw was brought as an emphasis on that. The better view is that this clause is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) for "qaryah," because it has the status of a qualifier, as if it were said: "And We did not destroy a town of the towns, not as a qualifier." His saying "a known decreed term" (kitābun maʿlūm) means: a written and known term, which is its appointed end that was written in the Preserved Tablet (al-lawḥ al-maḥfūẓ) and made clear. Do you not see to His saying...

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 15, verse 5:

﴿No nation can precede its term, nor can they delay it.﴾ That is, [its term] in the place of its Book (kitab). ﴿Nor can they delay it﴾: that is, from it. It is omitted because it is understood. He made the word "nation" (ummah) feminine at first, then referred to it in the masculine at the end, treating it according to its wording (lafz) and its meaning (ma'na).

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 15, verse 6:

﴿And they say﴾ — that is, the disbelievers — ﴿O you to whom the Reminder has been sent down﴾ — that is, the Qur'an — ﴿indeed you are surely a madman﴾. They mean Muhammad, upon him be peace. This address from them was in the manner of mockery, as Pharaoh said: ﴿Indeed your messenger who has been sent to you is surely a madman﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 27]. And how could they acknowledge the sending down of the Reminder upon him while attributing it to madness? The inversion in their speech is for the sake of mockery. Sarcasm (al-tahakkum) is permissible, and from it is ﴿So give them tidings of a painful punishment﴾ [Ali 'Imran: 21], and ﴿Indeed you are surely the forbearing, the rightly guided﴾ [Hud: 87]. The meaning is: indeed you speak the words of madmen, in that you claim that God has sent down the Reminder to you.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 15, verse 7:

﴿Why do you not bring us the angels, if you are among the truthful?﴾ "Law" (لَوْ) was combined with "lā" and "mā" to express the prevention of one thing because of the existence of another; or it is for urging (taḥḍīd); and "hal" was combined with "lā" for urging alone. The meaning is: "Why do you not bring us the angels bearing witness to your truthfulness?" or "Why do you not bring us the angels to punish us for our denial of you, if you are truthful?"

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 15, verse 8:

﴿We do not send down the angels﴾ — read by the Kufans except Abu Bakr; "Tunazzalu al-malaikatu" (the angels are sent down) is the reading of Abu Bakr; "Tanazzalu al-malaikatu" (the angels descend), i.e., tatanazzalu; the others (read it so). ﴿Except with truth﴾ — i.e., except a sending down mingled with wisdom. ﴿And they would not then be reprieved﴾ — "idhan" is an answer to them. The response to the conditional is implied, its sense being: "Even if We had sent down the angels, they would not have been reprieved then, and their punishment would not have been delayed."

**Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 15, verse 9:**

﴿Indeed, it is We who have sent down the Reminder﴾, that is, the Qur'an, ﴿and indeed We are its guardians﴾. This is a rejection of their denial and mockery in their saying, ﴿O you to whom the Reminder has been revealed﴾ [al-Hijr: 6]. For this reason He said "Indeed, it is We," emphasising to them definitively that He is the One who sent it down, and that He is the One who sent it down protected from the devils, and that He is its guardian at all times against addition, omission, distortion and alteration. This is unlike the earlier scriptures, for He did not undertake to preserve them. Rather, He entrusted their preservation to the rabbis (al-rabbaniyyun) and the scholars (al-ahbar), so they differed among themselves out of rebellion, and distortion occurred. He did not entrust the preservation of the Qur'an to anyone else. His saying "And indeed We are its guardians" has been taken as evidence that it is revealed from Him as a sign (ayah), for if it were the words of a human being or not a sign, addition and omission would enter it just as they enter every other speech. Alternatively, the pronoun in "lahu" (its) refers to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), as in His saying ﴿And Allah will protect you﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 67].

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 15, verse 10:

﴿And We certainly sent (messengers) before you among the sects of the former peoples.﴾ That is: And We certainly sent messengers before you to the factions of the former peoples. The shi'ah (a faction, a group) is a company of people who agree upon a doctrine (madhhab) and a way (tariqah).

(p-185)

Qur'anic quotations: ﴿وَما يَأْتِيهِمْ﴾ "And there does not come to them..."

Translation:

﴿And there came not to them﴾ is a narration of a past state, because "má" (the negative particle "mā") does not enter upon a present-tense verb except that it carries the meaning of the present state, and does not enter upon a past-tense verb except that it is close to the present state. ﴿any messenger but that they used to mock him﴾. He is consoling his Prophet, peace be upon him.

Thus do We cause it to enter into the hearts of the criminals. That is: just as We caused disbelief or mockery to enter among the sects of the earlier peoples, We cause it, i.e., disbelief or mockery, to enter into the hearts of the criminals from your nation, those who choose that. It is said: "I threaded (salaktu) the thread into the needle and I caused it to pass through (aslaktuhu)," meaning: when you insert it into it. And this is a proof against the Mu'tazilah concerning al-aslah (what is most beneficial for the servant) and the creation of acts.

Translation:

﴿They do not believe in it﴾ — in Allah, or in the Reminder (al-dhikr). This (clause) is a circumstantial clause (hal). ﴿And the way of the former peoples has already passed on﴾ — their practice (tariqa) which Allah instituted (sanna) in destroying them when they denied His messengers. And this is a warning (wa'id) to the people of Makkah for their denial.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 15, verse 14:

﴿Even if We opened to them a gate from the heaven﴾

And if We were to show them the clearest sign, which is the opening of a gate from the heaven, ﴿so that they continued to ascend through it﴾ — that is, they would be climbing up.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 15, verse 15:

﴿Had We opened for them a gate into the heaven, and they continued ascending through it, they would surely say: "Our eyes have only been dazzled (sukkirat). Rather, we are a people bewitched."﴾ "Ḥuyyirat" (were bewildered) or "ḥubisat" (were blocked) from seeing, from "al-sakr" (intoxication/stopping) or from "al-sakar" (intoxication). "Sukkirat" is read by Makki, meaning: they were blocked, as a river is blocked from flowing. The meaning is: these polytheists had reached such an extreme of obstinacy that, if a gate of the gates of the heaven were opened for them, and a ladder were made easy for them by which they might ascend to it, and they saw with their own eyes what they saw, they would still say that it is a thing we imagine, having no reality. And they would say ﴿Rather, we are a people bewitched﴾, Muhammad has bewitched us with this. Or the pronoun refers to the angels, meaning: if We showed them the angels ascending into the heaven plainly, they would say that. He mentioned the daytime (zulul) so that their ascent would be by day, so that they would be clearly perceiving what they see. And he said "innama" to indicate that they state definitively that this is nothing but the blinding of the eyes. (p-186)

﴿And We have certainly placed in the sky﴾ — We created in it ﴿constellations﴾ — stars, or (according to another view) mansions/fortresses in which there are guards — or stations for the stars; ﴿and We adorned it﴾ — that is, the sky — ﴿for the beholders﴾.
And We guarded it (i.e., the sky) from every accursed devil (shaytan rajim), meaning one who is cursed or stoned with shooting stars.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 15, verse 18:

﴿Except one who snatches a hearing﴾, i.e., what is heard. "Man" (مَنِ) is in the accusative position as an exception. ﴿Then he is pursued by a flaming shihab﴾: a star that shoots down and then returns. ﴿Clear﴾: evident to those who see.

It is said: They were not barred from all the heavens. When ʿIsa (ʿalayhi al-salam) was born, they were prevented from three heavens. When Muhammad (ﷺ) was born, they were prevented from all the heavens.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 15, verse 19:

﴿And the earth — We have spread it out﴾: we spread it out from beneath the Ka'bah. The majority (al-Jumhur) hold that He, exalted is He, spread it over the surface of the water. ﴿And We cast into it firm mountains﴾: in the earth, mountains that are fixed. ﴿And We caused to grow in it of every thing weighed out﴾: weighed by the balance of wisdom and measured by a measure that its nature requires, in which there is neither excess nor deficiency; or it has a weight and a measure in matters of benefit and blessing; or it refers to what is weighed, such as saffron, gold, silver, copper, iron and others. What is weighed was singled out because measuring by volume ends at weighing.

﴿And We have made for you therein﴾ on the earth ﴿means of subsistence﴾, that by which one lives of foods; it is the plural of maʿīshah, and it is written with a clear yāʾ, unlike al-khabāʾith (the foul things) and the like, for writing the yāʾ in them is an error. ﴿And [We made provision] for those for whom you are not providers﴾. Man (مَن) is in the accusative position by coordination with maʿāyish, or on the place of "lakum" (for you), as if it were said: "And We have made for you therein means of subsistence, and We have made for you those for whom you are not providers," or "We have made for you therein means of subsistence, and for those for whom you are not providers." By them is meant the dependants, the slaves, and the servants whom you think you provide for, but you are mistaken, for God is the Provider; He provides for them and for you. It includes livestock, beasts, and the like.

It is not permissible for the position of man (مَن) to be genitive by coordination with the pronoun in "lakum," because a genitive pronoun is coordinated upon only by repeating the preposition.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 15, verse 21:

﴿And there is not a thing but that with Us are its treasuries, and We do not send it down except in a known measure.﴾ The mention of "treasuries" is a figure of speech (tamthil), and the meaning is: there is no thing from which the servants benefit except that We are capable of bringing it into being, creating it, and bestowing it, and We give it only in a known measure. So He struck the treasuries as an example of His power over every thing that is within His capacity.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 15, verse 22:

﴿And We sent the winds fertilizing﴾ (lawāqiḥ, plural of lāqiḥah), meaning: We sent the winds carrying the clouds, because they carry the cloud within them as if they were pregnant (laqiḥah) with it, from laqihat al-nāqah, meaning she became pregnant. Its opposite is ʿaqīm (barren). "al-Riḥ" (the winds) is read by Ḥamzah. ﴿So We sent down water from the sky and gave you to drink from it﴾, meaning We made it for you a means of drink. ﴿And you are not its storers﴾. He negated from them what He affirmed for Himself in His saying: "And there is not a thing but its treasures are with Us" (Qur'an 15:21). It is as if He said: We are the ones who store the water, in the sense that We are the ones able to create it in the sky and send it down from it, and you are not capable of that, showing the greatness of His power and their incapacity.

Verse 23: "And indeed it is We who give life and cause death, and We are the Inheritors."

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil): ﴿And indeed it is We who give life and cause death﴾, meaning: We give life by bringing into existence, and We cause death by annihilation; or We cause death when the appointed terms come to an end, and We give life for the recompense of deeds, according to the order of prior and subsequent [mentioned] (ʿalā al-taqdīm wa-al-taʾkhīr), since the wāw (and) is for general conjunction without specifying order. ﴿And We are the Inheritors﴾, the ones who remain after the destruction of all creation. It has also been said that the word "inheritor" (wārith) is applied to the one who remains by metaphor (istiʿāra), borrowed from the inheritor of the deceased, because He remains after their annihilation.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 15, verse 24:

﴿And We certainly know those of you who go before, and We certainly know those who come later.﴾ (Those who precede in birth and death, and those who come later.) Or: those who have come forth from the loins of men and those who have not yet come forth; or those who precede in Islam, or in obedience, or in the front rank of the congregation, or the front rank of battle, and those who come later.

Qur'anic quotations in ﴿ ﴾ markers, translated plainly. Verse 15:25 is the passage's subject; the text here is the commentary on the verse.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 15, verse 25:

﴿And indeed, your Lord—it is He who will gather them﴾ That is: He alone has the power to gather them and encompasses their assembly. ﴿Indeed, He is All-Wise, All-Knowing﴾ — possessing perfect wisdom and far-reaching knowledge.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 15, verse 26:

﴿And We certainly created man﴾, i.e., Adam, ﴿from clay of sounding dry clay, unfired﴾, ﴿from black mud altered﴾, ﴿molded﴾. The phrase ﴿from black mud﴾ is a qualifier of ﴿sounding clay﴾, meaning: He created him "from sounding clay" which is "from black mud", i.e., black, altered clay, ﴿molded﴾, shaped. Initially, he was dust, then it was kneaded with water and became clay; then it remained and became black mud; then it was refined and became an extract (sulalah), then it was shaped and dried and became sounding clay, so there is no contradiction.

"And the jinn" — the father of the jinn, like Adam is to mankind — is Iblis. It is in the accusative, governed by a verb understood, which the following explains: "We created him before," i.e., before Adam, "from the fire of the samum," i.e., from the fire of intense heat that penetrates the pores pervasively. It has been said: this samum is one part of seventy parts of the samum of the fire from which Allah created the jinn.
﴿And when your Lord said﴾ — remember the time of His saying ﴿to the angels, "Indeed, I am creating a human being from clay, from black mud altered in smell."﴾

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 15, verse 29:

﴿So when I have proportioned him﴾ I have perfected his creation and prepared it for the breathing of the spirit into it. ﴿And breathed into him of My spirit﴾ I placed the spirit in him and gave him life. There is no actual "breathing" here; it is a figure of speech (tamthil), and the attribution (idafah) to Myself is for honour and distinction. ﴿Then fall down before him in prostration﴾ It is an imperative from waqa'a, yaqa'u (to fall), meaning: fall to the ground, that is, prostrate yourselves before him. The fa' (then) has entered because it is the response (jawab) of "idha" (when). This is evidence that the command may precede the time of the act.

﴿So the angels prostrated, all of them together.﴾ *Al-malāʾika* (the angels) is a general plural (*jamʿ ʿāmm*) which admits of *takhṣīṣ* (restriction to a part of its scope). So the door of restriction was closed by his saying *کُلُّهُمْ* ("kulluhum," "all of them"). Mentioning the whole (*al-kull*) admitted the interpretation of *tafarruq* (dispersal, i.e. that they prostrated separately, one after another), so he cut that off by saying *أجْمَعُونَ* ("ajmaʿūn," "together").

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 15, verse 31:

﴿Except Iblis﴾. The apparent sense of the exception indicates that he was one of the angels, because the excepted item (al-mustathna) must be of the same kind as that from which it is excepted (al-mustathna minhu). It is narrated from al-Hasan that the exception is discontinuous (munqati') and that he was not one of the angels. We say: one who was not commanded does not become cursed by abandoning (the command). In al-Kashshaf (al-Zamakhshari) it says: he was among them, commanded together with them to prostrate, so the name "angels" was applied to them by predominance (taghlib), and then the exception was made after this predominance, like your saying: "I saw them, except Hind."

﴿He refused to be with those who prostrate﴾: he refused that he should be with them. "Aba" (refused) is a resumptive clause (isti'naf) answering an implied question of someone who says: "Why did he not prostrate?" So it was said: he refused that and became arrogant towards it. It was also said that its meaning is: "But Iblis refused."

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 15, verse 32:

﴿He said, "O Iblis, what is [the matter] with you that you are not among those who prostrate?"﴾ The preposition "maʿa" (with) is [here] — though its object is omitted; its implied sense is: "What [reason] do you have for not being with those who prostrate?" That is: "What purpose do you have in your refusal to prostrate?"

﴿He said, "I would not be one to prostrate myself to a human whom You created from clay, from black mud altered in form."﴾ The lam (ل) here is for emphasizing the negation; meaning: "It is not proper for me to prostrate myself to..." ﴿to a human whom You created from clay, from black mud altered in form﴾

[Qur'an 15:34] He said, "Then get out of it, for indeed you are accursed (rajim)." — meaning: get out of it. Out of what? Out of the heavens, or out of the Garden, or out of the company of the angels. "For indeed you are accursed (rajim)": driven away (matrud) from the mercy of Allah; its meaning is cursed (mal'un), because cursing (la'na) is precisely being driven away from mercy and being removed far from it.

Quranic quotation: ﴿And upon you is the curse until the Day of Judgment﴾. The Day of Judgment is set as the limit of the curse, because it is the furthest end that people set in their speech. What is meant is: you are blameworthy, and cursed upon in the heavens and the earth until the Day of Judgment, without being punished; then when that day comes, you will be punished with something that makes the cursing of you be forgotten.

﴿He said, "My Lord, then grant me respite"﴾ (meaning: delay me)
﴿until the Day they are raised﴾

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 15, verses 37–38:

(p-190) He said, "Indeed, you are among those given respite" ﴿until the Day of the appointed time﴾. "The Day of Judgment" (yawm al-din), "the Day they are raised" (yawm yub'athun), and "the Day of the appointed time" (yawm al-waqt al-ma'lum) have one meaning, but the expressions were varied, following the path of eloquence (balagha) in speech. It was also said that he only asked for respite until the Day in which they are raised so that he would not die, because no one dies on the Day of Resurrection; so he was not granted that, and was given respite until the end of the days of obligation (al-taklif).

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 15, verses 37–38:

(p-190) He said, "Indeed, you are among those given respite" ﴿until the Day of the appointed time﴾. "The Day of Judgment" (yawm al-din), "the Day they are raised" (yawm yub'athun), and "the Day of the appointed time" (yawm al-waqt al-ma'lum) have one meaning, but the expressions were varied, following the path of eloquence (balagha) in speech. It was also said that he only asked for respite until the Day in which they are raised so that he would not die, because no one dies on the Day of Resurrection; so he was not granted that, and was given respite until the end of the days of obligation (al-taklif).

﴿He said: "My Lord, because You have led me astray"﴾. The bāʾ (ba) is for oath (qasam), and mā is a verbal-noun (maṣdariyyah) particle, and the answer of the oath is ﴿I will surely make [evil] attractive to them﴾. The meaning: "I swear by Your leading me astray, ﴿I will surely make [sins] attractive to them﴾." Similar to His saying ﴿by Your might I will surely mislead them all﴾ [Ṣād: 82] in that it is an oath; except that one of them is an oath by an attribute of the essence (ṣifat al-dhāt) and the other by an attribute of the act (ṣifat al-fiʿl). The jurists (fuqahāʾ) have distinguished between them: the Iraqis said that swearing by an attribute of the essence, such as power (qudrah), greatness (ʿaẓamah), or might (ʿizzah), is an oath (yamīn), while swearing by an attribute of the act, such as mercy (raḥmah) or wrath (sukhṭ), is not an oath. The more correct view is that oaths are based on custom (ʿurf): whatever people commonly swear by is an oath, and what they do not is not. The verse is a proof against the Muʿtazilah regarding the creation of acts (khalq al-afʿāl), and their interpreting it as mere causation (taslīb) is a deviation from the apparent meaning. ﴿On the earth﴾: in the world (dunyā), which is the abode of delusion (dār al-ghurūr). He intended: "I am able to deceive Adam and make eating from the tree attractive to him while he was in heaven; so I am even more able to make [sin] attractive to his offspring on the earth." ﴿And I will surely mislead them all﴾

﴿Illa ʿibādaka minhumu al-mukhlaṣīn﴾ — "except Your sincere servants among them." With the lam pronounced with a kasra (al-mukhlisīn, i.e. the lam read with a kasra, "those who make [themselves] sincere"): Basran, Meccan and Syrian readers. [The verse] made an exception of "the sincere ones" (al-mukhlaṣīn), because He knew that his scheming would have no effect on them and that they would not accept it from him.

This is the commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 15, verses 41–42:

﴿He said: "This is a path that leads straight to Me."﴾ ﴿Indeed, My servants, over them you have no authority, except for those who follow you of the misguided.﴾ That is: this is a true path incumbent upon Me to observe, namely that you shall have no authority over My servants, except for those among them who choose to follow you by their own error. It is also said that the meaning of "ʿalayya" (upon Me) is "ilayya" (toward Me). ("ʿAliyy") is read by Yaʿqub, from the loftiness of nobility and excellence.

﴿He said: "This is a path that leads straight to Me."﴾ ﴿Indeed, My servants, over them you have no authority, except for those who follow you of the misguided.﴾ That is: this is a true path incumbent upon Me to observe, namely that you shall have no authority over My servants, except for those among them who choose to follow you by their own error. It is also said that the meaning of "ʿalayya" (upon Me) is "ilayya" (toward Me). ("ʿAliyy") is read by Yaʿqub, from the loftiness of nobility and excellence.
"And indeed Hell is the promised place for them all." The pronoun refers to those who go astray (al-ghawun).

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 15, verse 44:

﴿It has seven gates; for each gate there is a portion of them⁠—﴾ from the followers of Iblis ﴿a designated portion⁠﴾, a known, separated share. It has been said: the gates of the Fire are its levels (atbaq, singular tabaq, "layers") and its degrees (adrak, singular darak, "tiers"). The highest of them is for the monotheists (muwahhidun), who are punished according to the measure of their sins and then come out. The second is for the Jews, the third for the Christians, the fourth for the Sabians (al-Sabi'un), the fifth for the Magians (al-Majus), the sixth for the polytheists (al-mushrikun), and the seventh for the hypocrites (al-munafiqun).

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 15, verse 45:

﴿Indeed, the God-fearing will be in gardens and springs.﴾ As for the vowelling of ʿuyūn (springs) with a ḍamma on the ʿayn (ʿuyūn, rather than ʿiyūn): Madanī, Baṣrī and Ḥafṣ read it so. Al-muttaqī ʿalā l-iṭlāq (the God-fearing in the absolute sense) is the one who guards against what must be guarded against of what has been prohibited. He said in al-Sharḥ: If the People of the Book are included in His words ﴿For it are seven gates, and for each gate is a portion allotted﴾, then what is meant by "the God-fearing" are those who avoided the major sins; otherwise, what is meant by it are those who avoided shirk.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 15, verse 46:

﴿Enter it﴾ i.e., it will be said to them: ﴿Enter it﴾. ﴿In peace﴾ is a circumstantial phrase (ḥāl), meaning: safe, or greeted with peace, the angels greeting you. ﴿Secure﴾ from being expelled from it and from calamities within it; this is another circumstantial phrase.

﴿And We will remove whatever resentment is in their breasts﴾, which is the hatred lodged in the heart. That is, if one of them had resentment against another in this world, Allah will remove it from their hearts in Paradise and purify their souls. It is related from Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, that he said: "I hope that I, Uthman, Talha and al-Zubayr will be among them." It was also said: its meaning is that Allah purifies their hearts from envying one another over the ranks in Paradise, removes from them every resentment, and places in them affection and mutual love. ﴿Brothers﴾ is a circumstantial state (ḥāl), the accusative word *إخوانًا* describing their condition. ﴿Upon couches facing one another﴾. Likewise, it was said: the couches turn with them wherever they turn, so that in all their states they are facing one another, each seeing the other. (p-192)

﴿They will not be touched therein by weariness﴾: in Paradise there is no toil. ﴿Nor will they be removed from it﴾: so the completion of the blessing is through eternal abiding (khulud). And when he had completed the mention of the promise and the warning, he followed it with what comes after.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 15, verse 49–50:

﴿Inform My servants that I am the Forgiving, the Merciful.﴾ ﴿And that My punishment is the painful punishment.﴾ This is a confirmation of what was mentioned and an establishing of it in souls. He (ﷺ) said: "If the servant knew the extent of God's pardon, he would not refrain from what is forbidden; and if he knew the extent of His punishment, he would exhaust himself in worship and would never commit a sin."

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 15, verse 49–50:

﴿Inform My servants that I am the Forgiving, the Merciful.﴾ ﴿And that My punishment is the painful punishment.﴾ This is a confirmation of what was mentioned and an establishing of it in souls. He (ﷺ) said: "If the servant knew the extent of God's pardon, he would not refrain from what is forbidden; and if he knew the extent of His punishment, he would exhaust himself in worship and would never commit a sin."

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 15, verse 51:

﴿And inform them﴾: that is, inform your community. He conjoined it to "Inform My servants" (so that they may take what He sent down of punishment upon the people of Lut as a lesson, by which they may consider the wrath of Allah and His vengeance upon the criminals, and so that they may be certain before Him that His punishment is the painful punishment), ﴿about the guests of Ibrahim﴾: that is, his guests. They were Jibril, peace be upon him, together with eleven angels. The word "dayf" (guest) may be used for one or for many, since it is a verbal noun (masdar) of "dafahu" (he hosted him).

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 15, verse 52:

﴿When they entered upon him and said, "Peace."﴾ That is: we greet you with peace, or we have said peace. ﴿He said﴾ — that is, Ibrahim — ﴿"Indeed, we are apprehensive of you."﴾ Fearful, because of their refraining from eating, or because they entered without permission and at an unseasonable time.

﴿They said, "Do not be afraid."﴾ "Do not fear."

﴿Indeed, We give you good news﴾ *istinaf* (a resumed sentence, a new clause) with the sense of *ta'lil* (causal explanation) for the prohibition against fear, meaning: you are one who is given good news and are safe, so do not be afraid. With the lightening and opening of the nun, reading *نُبَشِّرُكَ* as *nubashshiruka* with the first letter lightened and the nun opened, it is read by Hamzah.

﴿of a knowing boy﴾ He is Isaac, based on His saying in Surat Hud: ﴿So We gave her good news of Isaac﴾ [Hud: 71].

﴿He said, "Do you give me good tidings although old age has touched me?"﴾ That is: do you give me good tidings that a child will be born to me while old age has touched me? That is, childbearing is ordinarily something strange in old age. ﴿Then by what do you give good tidings?﴾ Here "ما" is the interrogative (*ma al-istifhamiyyah*), and the sense of wonder has entered into it, as if it were said: "Then by what marvel do you give good tidings?"

As for the reading with a kasra on the nun and a shaddah, it is that of Makki. The original form is تُبَشِّرُونَنِي (*tubashshirunnani*). The nun of the plural was assimilated into the nun of support (*nun al-'imad*, the nun that supports the first person pronoun), then the ya' was deleted and the kasra was left as evidence of it.

The reading تُبْشِرُونِ (*tubshirun*) with lightening is that of Nafi'. The original is تُبْشِرُونَنِي, so the ya' was deleted, relying on the kasra, and the nun of the plural was deleted because two nuns came together.

The rest read with a fatha on the nun, and the object is deleted, and the nun is the nun of the plural.

(p-193)
﴿They said, "We give you good news of the truth"﴾ — that is, of certainty about which there is no doubt. ﴿So do not be among the despairing﴾ — that is, among those who have lost hope in that.

Ibrahim said: "And who despairs of the mercy of his Lord, except those who are astray?"

The reading with a kasra on the nun (وَمَن يَكْسِرُ النون) is that of Basri and Ali. [The Arabic here is "يَقْنَطُ" with the nun vowelled with a kasra, which is the reading of Ibn Kathir's companions from Basra and of Ali, i.e., al-Kisa'i.]

"Except those who are astray" means: except those who err from the right path. Or it means: except the disbelievers, as in His words: ﴿Indeed, no one despairs of the mercy of Allah except the disbelieving people﴾ [Yusuf: 87]. The meaning is: I did not regard this as despair of His mercy, but as an unlikely event, given the customary way in which He operates.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 15, verse 57:

﴿He said, "Then what is your business, O messengers?"﴾ That is, what is your matter (fa-ma sha'nukum), ﴿O messengers﴾?

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 15, verse 58:

﴿They said: "Indeed, we have been sent to a people who are criminals."﴾ That is: the people of Lot.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 15, verse 59:

﴿Except the family of Lot﴾ means his believing family. The exception (istithna') is disjunctive (munqati'), because the people are described by criminality (ijram) while the excepted party is not so described. Or it is conjunctive (muttasil), in which case it is an exception from the pronoun in "criminals" (mujrimin), as if it were said: "To a people who have all committed crime, except the family of Lot alone." The meaning differs according to the two kinds of exception. For the family of Lot, in the disjunctive case, are excluded from the ruling of the sending (irsal): that is, they were sent only to the criminal people specifically, and were not sent to the family of Lot at all. The meaning of their being sent to the criminal people is like the sending of an arrow to its target, in that it carries the sense of punishment and destruction, as if it were said: "We destroyed a criminal people, but the family of Lot We saved." In the conjunctive case, however, they are included within the ruling of the sending, that is: the angels were sent to them all, to destroy these and to save those. When the exception is disjunctive, ﴿Indeed, We will surely save them all﴾ functions in the position of the predicate of inna (khabar inna) in relation to the family of Lot, because the meaning is "but the family of Lot are saved." When it is conjunctive, it is a resumed statement (kalam mustani'af), as if Abraham, peace be upon him, said to them: "Then what is the state of the family of Lot?" and they said: "Indeed, We will surely save them."

The phrase ﴿except his wife﴾ is an exception from the pronoun in "لَمُنَجَّوْهُمْ" (lamunajjawhum, "We will surely save them"), and it is not an exception from an exception (istithnāʾ min al-istithnāʾ). An exception from an exception (istithnāʾ, meaning exception) applies only where the ruling is the same throughout. For example, one would say: "We destroyed them, except the family of Lūṭ, except his wife." Here the two rulings differ. "Āl Lūṭ" (the family of Lūṭ) is linked to "arsalnā" (We sent) or to "mujrimīn" (criminals), while "illā imra'atahu" (except his wife) is linked to "munajjūhum" (We will save them). So how could it be an exception from an exception?

"Lamunjūhum" with light vowelling (takhfīf) is read by Ḥamzah and ʿAlī. "Qaddarnā" (We decreed) with the doubled letter is read by Abū Bakr. ﴿Surely she is among those who remain behind﴾, meaning those who remain in the punishment. It has been said: if the lām were not in its predicate, then the hamza of "innahā" would have to be pronounced with a fatḥa (inna would become anna), because it, together with its subject and predicate, is the object of "qaddarnā." But it is like His saying: ﴿And the jinn certainly knew that they would be brought [to judgment]﴾ [al-Ṣāffāt: 158]. The angels attributed the act of decreeing to themselves and did not say "God decreed," because of their closeness [to God], just as the close attendants of a king say: "We have ordered such-and-such," while the one who gives the order is the king.

**Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on Surah 15, verses 61–62:**

﴿When the messengers came to the family of Lot﴾ ﴿he said, "Indeed, you are a people unknown to me."﴾ That is: "I do not know you." That is: you do not wear the dress of travelers, nor are you of the people of settled residence, so I fear that you may come upon me with evil.

**Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on Surah 15, verses 61–62:**

﴿When the messengers came to the family of Lot﴾ ﴿he said, "Indeed, you are a people unknown to me."﴾ That is: "I do not know you." That is: you do not wear the dress of travelers, nor are you of the people of settled residence, so I fear that you may come upon me with evil.

"They said: Nay, we have brought you that about which they used to doubt."

That is: we have not brought you what you deny us for, but we have brought you that in which lies your joy and the satisfaction of your heart against your enemies, namely the punishment which you used to threaten them with its descent, so they doubt it (yamtarun fihi), that is: they are in doubt about it and they deny you.
﴿And We have certainly brought you the truth﴾ — with certainty concerning their punishment. ﴿And indeed We are truthful﴾ — in reporting its descent upon them.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 15, verse 65:

﴿So set out with your family in the last part of the night⌋ at the end of the night, or after some portion of the night has passed (p-195) ﴿and follow behind them⌋ and go behind them so that you may keep watch over them and their circumstances ﴿and let none of you look back⌋ lest they see the punishment that is about to befall their people, and so feel pity for them. Or the prohibition against looking back is taken as a metaphor (kinaya) for continuing the journey without slackening or stopping, because whoever looks back must necessarily pause for at least a brief moment ﴿and proceed to where you are commanded⌋ to where Allah has commanded you to proceed, which is al-Sham (Syria) or Misr (Egypt).

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 15, verse 66:

﴿And We decreed that matter to him﴾. He used "qadayna" with "ila" because it was made to imply the meaning of "awhayna" (We revealed), as if it were said: "And We revealed to him that the matter was decreed and settled." That matter is explained by His words ﴿that the last of these will be cut off﴾. In leaving it vague and then explaining it there is an emphasis on the gravity of the matter. "Dabiruhum" means their last (remnant), i.e., they will be uprooted down to the last of them, so that not one of them remains. ﴿at daybreak﴾: at the time of their entering into the morning (ṣubḥ), and it is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) referring to "hā'ulā'" (these people).
﴿The people of the city came﴾, Sodom (Sadum), whose judge was proverbial for injustice, ﴿rejoicing﴾ at the angels, hoping to commit the abomination with them.
Lot said: ﴿Indeed, these are my guests, so do not disgrace me﴾ by disgracing my guests, for whoever wrongs my guest has wronged me.
﴿So fear Allah and do not disgrace me.﴾ That is: do not humiliate me by humiliating my guests. Al-khizy (disgrace) means abasement (al-hawan). The reading with a yāʾ (ي) in it is that of Yaʿqub.

They said, "Did we not forbid you from the people of the worlds?" That is, from giving protection to any of them or defending them from harm, for they used to molest everyone. He, peace be upon him, would enjoin what is reprehensible (al-munkar) and stand between them and whoever molested them. So they threatened him and said, ﴿If you do not desist, O Lut, you will surely be among those expelled﴾ [al-Shu'ara: 167]. Or the meaning is: forbidding him from hosting strangers. (p-196)

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 15, verse 71:

﴿He said: "These are my daughters, if you must act (so)."﴾ So marry them. It was permissible for believing women to be married to disbelievers, and do not confront them. ﴿If you must act﴾ means: if you want to fulfil desire in what Allah has made lawful, rather than what He has forbidden. Then the angels said to Lut, peace be upon him.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 15, verse 72:

﴿By your life, indeed they are in their intoxication﴾ i.e., in their misguidance, which has taken away their intellects and their discernment between the error they are upon and the correctness to which you point them, namely abandoning sons for daughters, ﴿wandering blindly﴾, bewildered. So how would they accept your words or lend an ear to your counsel?

Or the address is to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and it is an oath by his life, (an oath) glorifying him, and (the Arabs) never swore by the life of anyone at all. ʿUmr and ʿUmr (both pronounced with the vowel variations) are one and the same, meaning "lifetime" or "remaining (in existence)," except that they restricted the oath to the open (fatha-vowelled) form, preferring the lighter form because the oath occurs so often on their tongues. For this reason they omitted the predicate, and its implied form is: "By your life, my oath."
﴿So the Cry seized them﴾, the Cry of Jibril (peace be upon him), ﴿at sunrise﴾, meaning those who entered into الشروق (ash-shuruq), which is the rising of the sun.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 15, verse 74:

﴿So We made its highest part its lowest⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠ ﴾ Jibril (upon him be peace) lifted them up to the sky, then overturned them. The pronoun refers to the towns of the people of Lut. ﴿And We rained upon them stones of baked clay⁠﴾

﴿Indeed in that are signs for those who discern.﴾ That is, for those who look closely (al-mutafarrisin) and reflect (al-mutaammilin), as if they know the inner reality of a thing through an outward mark (simah).

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 15, verse 76:

﴿And indeed, it﴾ — and indeed these towns, meaning their remains, ﴿are on a road that remains﴾ — a established path which people travel, not yet effaced, and they see those remains. This is a warning to the Quraysh, as in His saying: ﴿And indeed you pass by them in the morning﴾ [al-Saffat: 137] ﴿and at night﴾ [al-Saffat: 138].
Indeed, in that is a sign for the believers (﴿Indeed, in that is a sign for the believers﴾), because they are the ones who benefit from it.

"And indeed, the companions of the Thicket were surely wrongdoers" (﴿وَإنْ كانَ أصْحابُ الأيْكَةِ لَظالِمِينَ﴾)

And indeed the matter and the affair: "the companions of the Thicket" — i.e., the thicket (al-ghaydah) — ﴿were surely wrongdoers﴾ — meaning disbelievers (lakafirin). They were the people of Shu'ayb, peace be upon him. (p-197)

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 15, verse 79:

﴿So We took vengeance upon them﴾: We destroyed them when they denied Shu'ayb. ﴿And indeed they both﴾: meaning the towns of the people of Lot and the Aykah (the Thicket), ﴿are on a clear highway﴾: on a plain, evident path. Imam (imam, a leader or guide) is the name of that which one follows, so the path was named after it, and also the (building's) leveling line (miṭmar al-bina'), because both of them are things that are followed.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 15, verse 80:

﴿And the companions of al-Hijr denied the messengers.﴾ They are Thamud, and al-Hijr is their valley, which lies between Medina and Syria. "The messengers" means: by their denying Salih. For every messenger used to call to belief in all the messengers, so whoever denies one of them is as though he denied them all. Or [the intended meaning is] Salih and those believers who were with him, as it is said: "al-Khubaybiyyun" (the followers of Khubayb), regarding Ibn al-Zubayr and his companions.
"And We gave them Our signs, but they were turning away from them" (Q. 15:81). That is: they turned away from them and did not believe in them.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 15, verse 82:

﴿And they used to hew out dwellings from the mountains, secure.﴾ That is: they would bore out dwellings in the mountains, or build them of stone. ﴿Secure﴾ because of the solidity and firmness of the dwellings, that they would not collapse, and because of the breaching of thieves and enemies. Or "secure" (āminīn) from the punishment of Allah, thinking that the mountains would protect them from it.
﴿So the Cry seized them﴾, meaning the punishment, ﴿at dawn﴾, on the fourth day, at the time of morning.
Quranic quotation: ﴿So what they had been earning did not avail them﴾ — referring to what they earned from building sturdy houses and acquiring precious wealth.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 15, verse 85:

﴿And We did not create the heavens and the earth and what is between them except with truth.﴾ Except as a creation bound up with truth, not as falsehood and purposelessness; or for the sake of justice and fair dealing, on the Day of Recompense for deeds. ﴿And indeed the Hour﴾, that is, the Resurrection, [is so named] because of the expectation of it at every moment, ﴿is surely coming.﴾ And indeed Allah will avenge you upon your enemies in it, and will requite you and them for your good deeds and their evil deeds, for He did not create the heavens and the earth and what is between them except for that. ﴿So forgive with gracious forgiveness.﴾ That is, turn away from them with a beautiful turning away (p-198), with forbearance and overlooking. It has been said: it is abrogated by the verse of the sword; but if by it is meant mere opposition, then it is not abrogated.

Indeed your Lord is the Creator (al-Khallaq), the One who created you and them, the All-Knowing (al-'Alim) of your state and their state, so nothing that passes between you and them is hidden from Him, and He will judge between you.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 15, verse 87:

﴿And We have certainly given you seven [oft-repeated]﴾, i.e., seven verses, and these are al-Fatiha (the Opening), or seven surahs, and these are the long surahs (al-tiwal). It has been disputed what the seventh is. It was said: al-Anfal and Bara'a (al-Tawba), because they are in the ruling of one surah, as evidence by the absence of the basmala between them. It was also said: Surah Yunus, or "the sevens of the Qur'an" (asba' al-Qur'an).

﴿of the oft-repeated (al-mathani)﴾: it is from al-tathniya (doubling), which is repetition, because al-Fatiha is among what is repeated in the prayer. Or it is from al-thana' (praise), because it includes what is praise of Allah. The singular is mathna'a or mathniyya, an adjective of "ayah" (verse). As for the long surahs (al-asba' al-suwar), it is because of the repetition in them of stories, admonitions, promise and threat, and because of the praise in them, as if they praise Allah. If you make "the seven" to be "al-mathani," then "min" is for specification (li-l-tabyin); and if you make "the Qur'an" to be "al-mathani," then "min" is for partitive (li-l-tab'id).

﴿and the Glorious Qur'an﴾: this is not the conjoining of a thing with itself, because if by "the seven" is meant al-Fatiha or the long surahs, then what follows them is called by the name "Qur'an," since it is a name that applies to a part as it applies to the whole. Its evidence is His saying: "By what We have revealed to you of this Qur'an" (12:3), meaning Surah Yusuf. And if by it is meant the sevens, then the meaning is: We have given you that which is called "the seven oft-repeated," and "the Glorious Qur'an," i.e., the one comprising these two attributes, which are repetition (tathniya) or praise (thana') and greatness ('izam). Then He said to His Messenger:

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 15, verse 88:

﴿Do not strain your eyes﴾ meaning: do not direct your gaze with the aspiration of one who desires it and wishes for it. ﴿Toward what We have given enjoyment to some pairs of them﴾, categories of the disbelievers such as the Jews, the Christians and the Magians. The meaning is: you have been given the great blessing, and every blessing, however great, is petty compared to it, namely the Great Qur'an. So you should be content with it and not strain your eyes toward the goods of this world.

In the hadith: "He is not of us who does not chant the Qur'an melodiously" (ليس منا من لم يتغن بالقرآن). And the hadith of Abu Bakr (p-199): "Whoever has been given the Qur'an and sees that someone has been given something of this world better than what he has been given has belittled something great and magnified something small."

﴿And do not grieve over them﴾, meaning: do not covet their wealth, and do not grieve over them that they have not believed, so that Islam and the Muslims might be strengthened by their position. ﴿And lower your wing to the believers﴾, and be humble toward those of the poor believers who are with you, and be content in your soul regarding the faith of the wealthy.
**﴿And say﴾** to them, **﴿Indeed, I am the clear warner﴾**, warning you with clear explanation and proof that the punishment of Allah is descending upon you.

Ṣ: "As We sent down" is connected to His words "And We have certainly given you," meaning: We sent down to you the like of what We sent down **upon the al-Muqtasimin** (ﷺ), and they are the People of the Book.

Here is the translation with the required conventions applied:

"As We sent down" is connected to His words, "And We have certainly given you" (the seven often-repeated verses and the Great Qur'an), meaning: We sent down to you the like of what We sent down upon the **al-Muqtasimun** (those who divided), and they are the People of the Book.

The commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 15, verse 91:

﴿Those who have made the Qur'an into ʿiḍīn (fragments)﴾: ʿiḍīn means parts, the plural of ʿiḍah (ﻋِﻀَّﺔٍ). Its original form is ʿiḍwah, on the pattern fiʿlah, from ʿaḍḍā al-shāh (عَضّى الشاةَ), meaning when one divides a sheep into pieces (aʿḍāʾ, أعْضاءً). They said, out of their obstinacy: "Part of it is true, agreeing with the Tawrah (Torah) and the Injil (Gospel), and part of it is false, opposing them." So they divided it into true and false, and "ʿaḍawhu" (عَضَوْهُ) means they broke it into parts.

It was also said: they used to mock it. One of them would say, "Sūrat al-Baqarah is mine," and another would say, "Sūrat Āl ʿImrān is mine."

Or the meaning of al-Qur'an here is what they read from their own books, and they had divided that too. The Jews affirmed some of the Tawrah and denied some of it, and the Christians affirmed some of the Injil and denied some of it.

It is also permissible for "those who have made the Qur'an ʿiḍīn" to be in the accusative case, governed by "al-nadhīr" (the warner), meaning: warn the ones who divide the Qur'an (al-muʿiḍḍīn), those who break the Qur'an into sorcery, poetry and fables, ﴿like what We sent down upon the muqtasimīn (those who divided it)﴾. These were the twelve who divided the entrances of Makkah during the season (of pilgrimage). They sat at every entrance, dispersed, to turn people away from faith in the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). One of them would say, "Do not be deceived by the one who comes out from us, for he is a sorcerer." Another would say, "He is a liar," and another, "He is a poet." So Allah destroyed them.

﴿And do not extend your eyes﴾ on the first interpretation is a parenthetical interjection between the two parts, because when that was a consolation for the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) concerning their denial and enmity, it interjected with what is the basis of the meaning of consolation: the prohibition against turning one's attention to their worldly life and grieving over their disbelief, and the command to turn wholeheartedly to the believers (p-200).

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 15, verses 92–93:

﴿So by your Lord, We will surely question them all﴾ ﴿about what they used to do﴾. He swore by His own essence and His lordship that on the Day of Resurrection He would question each and every one of these dividers (al-muqtasimin) about what they had said concerning the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), or concerning the Qur'an, or concerning the books of Allah.

﴿So by your Lord, We will surely question them all﴾ ﴿about what they used to do﴾. He swore by His own essence and His lordship that on the Day of Resurrection He would question each and every one of these dividers (al-muqtasimin) about what they had said concerning the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), or concerning the Qur'an, or concerning the books of Allah.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 15, verse 94:

﴿So proclaim openly what you are commanded﴾ — that is, declare it and make it manifest. It is said: "ṣadaʿa bil-ḥujjah" (he delivered the proof openly) when one speaks with it plainly, from al-ṣadīʿ, which is the dawn. Or [it means] "fa-ṣdaʿ": separate, distinguish between the truth and falsehood, from al-ṣadʿ (splitting) in glass, which is clarification. "Bimā tu'mar" (what you are commanded): the meaning is "what you are commanded with of the sacred laws," so the preposition has been elided, as in his saying:

﴿؎ I commanded you the good, so do what you have been commanded with﴾

﴿And turn away from the polytheists﴾ — this is a command of disdain toward them.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 15, verse 95:

﴿Indeed, We suffice you against the mockers.﴾ The majority (al-Jumhur) hold that it was revealed concerning five men who were excessive in harming the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and in mocking him. So Allah destroyed them: al-Walid ibn al-Mughira passed by an arrow-maker (nabbal), and an arrow caught on his garment, struck a vein in his heel, and cut it, so he died. Al-'As ibn Wa'il had a thorn enter his sole, his foot swelled, and he died. Al-Aswad ibn 'Abd al-Muttalib went blind. Al-Aswad ibn 'Abd Yaghuth began striking his head against a tree and hitting his face with thorns until he died. Al-Harith ibn Qays expelled pus from his nose (imtakhata qayhan) and died.
﴿Those who set up another god alongside Allah, they will come to know﴾ the outcome of their affair on the Day of Resurrection. (p. 201)

**Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 15, verse 97:**

﴿And We certainly know that your breast is constricted by what they say﴾, [i.e., concerning you] or concerning the Qur'an or concerning Allah.

So glorify your Lord with His praise and be among those who prostrate. ﴿So glorify your Lord with His praise, and be among those who prostrate.﴾ Have recourse to God in what befalls you—and having recourse to God is constant remembrance (dhikr) and abundant prostration (sujud)—and He will suffice you and remove distress from you.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 15, verse 99:

﴿And worship your Lord﴾ and persist in the worship of your Lord ﴿until there comes to you the certainty﴾, i.e., death. The meaning is: as long as you are alive, occupy yourself with worship. "And whenever the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was faced with a grave matter, he would turn to prayer."
